summary: Lumi is an on-board health companion for astronauts far from Earth. It compares each new measurement with the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline, confirms any anomaly with a repeat measurement, and then guides the crew step by step through a protocol adapted to the problem, its severity and the mission environment (ISS, Moon or Mars), including when to contact the crew medical officer or flight surgeons and how long Earth takes to answer. It covers two risks studied by NASA's Human Research Program: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and loss of muscle size, strength and endurance. Lumi, an animated mascot, reads every step aloud. It guides; it does not diagnose. This matters because on long missions help from Earth can take many minutes, so the crew must spot slow health changes early and respond safely on their own.
details:
What it does. On long missions the crew has to notice health changes and respond before Earth can answer: a one-way signal between Mars and Earth takes about 3 to 22 minutes. Lumi focuses on two risks studied by NASA's Human Research Program: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) and loss of muscle size, strength and endurance.

How it works. The astronaut picks who they are and where the mission is (ISS, Moon or Mars). Grouped check-ins (eye scan, optic disc, refraction, visual acuity, grip strength, muscle size, power, endurance, tone and stiffness) record 14 indicators. Each value is compared with that astronaut's personal pre-flight baseline (mean and spread), so limits adapt to each body. Rules written by our health lead, with their sources, turn values into symptom levels (watch / concern) and a problem state. Any alert is confirmed with a repeat measurement before anything else happens. A confirmed alert opens a step-by-step protocol (questions, actions, measurements, contacts) drawn as a flowchart; urgent routes change with the environment and show the communication delay with Earth. Astronauts can also report subjective symptoms; urgent ones (for example sudden vision loss) show an immediate action. Trends plot every indicator against the personal baseline, Tutorials let the crew practise each protocol without saving anything, and progress bars driven by simulated mission time remind them what is due.

Benefits and impact. Earlier detection of slow changes, fewer false alarms (personal baseline plus repeat confirmation), clear guidance when Earth cannot answer in time, and a design that grows by adding new protocol files. Lumi, an animated mascot drawn in code, changes colour with the astronaut's state (blue nominal, amber follow-up, red urgent) and reads every step aloud, so the app can be followed mid-task.

Tools. Python 3.12, Streamlit, pandas, Plotly, Graphviz and pytest (over 1,300 automated tests). The mascot is drawn in SVG/CSS/JS and speaks with the browser's own speech synthesis. Deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud: https://nasa-health-monitor-jyjqxq9oyta7gece258ben.streamlit.app/ . All demo data is synthetic; each visitor works on their own copy.

Try it in 1 minute. Astronaut A, International Space Station, then Main Menu, Demo controls: Reset demo, Advance mission 24 h. Open Check-in, Simulate wait, repeat the flagged value with 360, confirm, and follow the protocol.

Limits. Lumi is a prototype, not a medical device: it guides and explains, and diagnosis stays with the crew medical officer and flight surgeons. Thresholds combine published criteria with the team's documented prototype choices; every source is listed in the repository README.
